client: I've been feeling really off ever since my breakup with Maria about three months ago. Like, things I used to love doing, hiking with friends, being outdoors, just don't feel the same anymore. I honestly don't know if talking about it is going to change anything, but I figured I'd give this a shot.
therapist: It means a lot that you took this step, even with some doubt about whether it will help — that kind of honesty is actually a really good starting point. Losing a relationship can quietly reshape the way everyday things feel, like the color has been turned down on experiences that used to light you up. I'm curious — when you're out on a hike or with friends now, what kinds of thoughts tend to run through your mind in those moments?

client: Yeah, when I'm out hiking or whatever, I keep thinking about how she would have loved this trail, or how I'd be taking a photo to send her. It's like my brain won't just let me be present — it keeps pulling me back to this person who isn't there anymore. And then I feel kind of guilty for even being out enjoying myself, like I don't deserve to feel good when things ended the way they did.
therapist: What you're describing makes so much sense — your brain formed deep habits around sharing experiences with Maria, and those habits don't just switch off overnight. I want to gently shine a light on that guilt though, because there's an interesting thought hiding in there: the idea that you *don't deserve* to feel good, which is worth examining together. What do you think "the way things ended" says about you as a person that would make feeling joy somehow off-limits for you?

client: I guess... when things ended with Maria, I was the one who pulled away first. I told myself it was for good reasons, but there's this voice in the back of my head that says I gave up on her, and people who give up on others don't really deserve to just move on and be happy. It feels like feeling joy would be some kind of proof that I didn't care enough in the first place.
therapist: That inner voice is carrying a really heavy judgment — essentially putting you on trial and ruling that happiness is off-limits as a kind of punishment. But I'd gently ask you to examine the logic there: is it actually true that someone who genuinely *didn't* care would feel this much pain and guilt three months later? What might it say about you that this still weighs on you so deeply?

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to accept that logic... but it almost feels too convenient, like I'm just looking for a way to let myself off the hook. Because yeah, I still feel the pain, but couldn't that just mean I feel bad about what I did rather than proving I actually cared about her? I'm not sure those two things are the same, and that distinction keeps tripping me up.
therapist: That's actually a really sharp and honest distinction to make, and it shows a lot of self-awareness that you're not just grabbing onto the easiest explanation. You're right that guilt and love aren't the same thing — but I'm wondering if the story that you "gave up on her" is the whole truth, or whether it's one harsh interpretation of a decision that probably had more complexity to it. What were those reasons you told yourself at the time when you pulled away — do they feel completely invalid to you now, or is part of you still able to see why you made that choice?

client: I mean... at the time I told myself I was drowning too, that I couldn't keep being her emotional support when I could barely hold myself together. And honestly, part of me still sees that — like, I wasn't in a good place, and I genuinely didn't know how to help her without losing myself. But then she died, and suddenly that reasoning feels like just a really convenient excuse I made up to justify abandoning someone who needed me.
therapist: I'm so sorry — losing Maria, and carrying this weight in the wake of her death, is an enormous amount of pain to hold. What you're experiencing now makes deep sense: grief has a way of rewriting our memories and turning reasonable, human decisions into evidence of the worst things we fear about ourselves. I want to sit with you in this for a moment — because the person who pulled away to protect their own mental health, and the person who genuinely cared about Maria, can both be true at the same time. Can you tell me a little about what it's been like carrying this since she passed?

client: It's been... exhausting, honestly. Like I wake up every morning and the first thing my brain does is replay all the times I didn't answer her calls, or made excuses not to visit, and I just lie there feeling like a terrible person before the day even starts. And the worst part is there's no way to fix it now — she's gone, and I can't go back and be the friend she deserved.
therapist: The finality of her death has locked you in a kind of impossible loop — your mind keeps returning to the evidence for the prosecution, with no way to take action or make amends, and that helplessness is one of the most painful places a person can be. I want to reflect something back to you gently: you're describing yourself as a "terrible person," but what I'm hearing is someone who was genuinely struggling, made imperfect choices under that strain, and is now grieving both Maria *and* the relationship you wish you'd had with her. I'm wondering — if a close friend came to you carrying this exact story, word for word, would you look at them and see a terrible person, or would you see something more complicated than that?

client: I've heard that question before, you know — the "what would you say to a friend" thing — and I always know what I'm supposed to say. But when I try to actually apply it to myself, it just... doesn't stick. Like I can see the logic of it, but it doesn't reach whatever part of me is convinced I failed her.
therapist: You're pointing to something really important — there's a difference between understanding something intellectually and actually *feeling* it, and it sounds like the part of you that believes you failed Maria isn't really a thoughts problem, it's deeper than that. That inner conviction probably didn't form through logic, which means logic alone isn't always enough to loosen its grip — sometimes it needs something different, like grief that's actually been felt and moved through rather than managed. I'm curious, in these three months, have you had any space to just *grieve* Maria — not analyze what happened or put yourself on trial, but actually mourn losing her?

client: I've been sitting with that question and honestly... I don't think I have. Every time I start to feel something about losing her, it immediately turns into this courtroom in my head where I'm listing everything I did wrong, and the grief just gets swallowed up by the guilt. I'm not even sure I know how to separate the two at this point.
therapist: What you just named is really significant — the guilt has essentially been standing guard at the door, not letting the grief through, and that means you've been carrying the weight of losing her without ever really getting to just *miss* her. That courtroom in your mind serves a kind of purpose, painful as it is — focusing on what you did wrong might actually feel safer than facing the rawness of simply loving someone who is gone. I wonder, if we could somehow quiet the prosecutor for just a moment — what would be the first thing you'd want to say to Maria, if you could?

client: I sat with that for a second and it actually kind of hit me hard, what you said about the guilt being a guard. Because you're right, it's easier to be angry at myself than to just... feel how much I miss her. If I could say something to Maria right now, I think it would just be "I'm sorry I wasn't there more, but I really did love you" — and even saying that out loud makes my chest tight in a way that's different from the guilt, it's just pure sadness.
therapist: That tightness in your chest right now — that's grief, real and uncomplicated, and it's actually a sign that you're finally letting yourself feel something true about her rather than about your own failures. What you just said, that you loved her, isn't in conflict with the choices you made when you were struggling — both things lived in you at the same time then, and they still do now. I want to ask you to stay with that feeling for just a moment rather than rushing past it — what's it like to let yourself simply miss her, even just for right now?

client: It's... strange, because when I actually let myself just miss her instead of immediately going to what I did wrong, there's this sadness that feels almost quieter somehow, less jagged. Like it's just her face I'm thinking about, the way she'd laugh at her own jokes before she even got to the punchline. But I don't know how long I can stay there before my brain pulls me back to the guilt, it's like it won't let me have the grief without the punishment attached to it.
therapist: What you just described — her laugh, her face — that's love, and it's yours to keep, and no amount of guilt can actually take that away from you. The fact that the sadness felt quieter and less jagged is really important information, because it suggests that the grief itself isn't what's unbearable — it's the guilt layered on top of it that makes it so sharp and exhausting. I'm wondering if we could think of that quieter place not as something you have to hold onto perfectly, but as somewhere you now know exists — a place you've visited once today and can find your way back to — does that feel like something worth gently practicing?
